messages.subject_clean: Two robust fit measures with MLR
messages.body_plain:
Dear professor Jorgensen, thank you for a quick reply and the literature.
Reading these papers you gave, I too would expect a citation for robust incremental fit indices ("robust CFI") or specific statement to avoid confusion, whereas I would expect to find scaled ones if an author reported only "CFI" or "RMSEA" obtained under some robust ML estimation without a citation or without specifying that they are robust ones - the majority of papers I see.  But I had to check whether I am unaware of research practice that goes on (i.e. switching scaled for robust without saying so).  Especially since I do not know what other programs give in their outputs while lavaan provides all (so I thought you were the guys to ask).

Thank you once again.

The issue of "causal relationship" is more complex that that. If you only have pre and post intervention, you still cannot state causality. As a minimum you need a control group for comparison

Now, with that type of data I recomened the latent change score model as

mod_ch_tot <- '
tot_post ~ 1*tot_pre
change =~ 1*tot_post

change ~c(m1)*1
change ~~ c(v1)*change

tot_post ~~ 0*tot_post
tot_post ~0*1

change ~~ tot_pre

### cohen d
cd1 := m1/sqrt(v1)
'

messages.body_plain:
Wang,
  Shadish, Cook & Campbell (2002) discuss the design you describe as a Single-Group Pretest-Posttest Design.  They discuss strengths and limitations, and also conditions that moderate valid causal inference.  However, in general, this is a weak design.  See Chapter 4 for details.  Control groups offer one way to strengthen the design, but not the only way.  Shadish, Cook and Campbell assume that the researcher is not in possession of complete knowledge of all the causal relations relevant to the two variables of interest.  Much current work on causal inference in focused on exploring available inferences when such complete knowledge is available to the researcher.  Under such circumstances, the design can be sufficient for estimating causal effect sizes.  However, these methods do not apply if the research it in the phase of figuring out the qualitative causal structure.

Keith

Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D. & Campbell, D. T. (2002).   Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference.  Boston:  Houghton Mifflin.

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
> lavaan WARNING:
>     The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
>     does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
>     (= -2.167349e-17) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
>     the model is not identified.
>
> Despite this, the model produces what seems like a sensible solution:

That's why it is a warning, not an error.  The smallest eigenvalue is essentially zero, not substantially negative, so this is probably ignorable.  Given you have 3+ items uniquely defining each factor, I don't see an obvious identification problem.

>   lavaan WARNING: estimation of the baseline model failed.

This means what it says.  A new feature of lavaan is that it tries fitting the default baseline model after fitting your model, so it can store the result in "fit".  That way, the baseline model doesn't have to be fit each time you call summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE) or fitMeasures(fit) to calculate CFI etc.  This has nothing to do with your hypothesized model, so you can ignore it.

> > reliability(fit)
> Error: $ operator not defined for this S4 class

Ugh, this stupid error only occurs for categorical data, when a hidden function calls fitted(fit).  For whatever reason, within the scope of the function, the correct fitted() method is not selected for lavaan objects.  I addressed this error in the reliability() function itself, but did not correct it in the hidden function for retrieving thresholds.  Corrected now in the development version:

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Thanks for catching it.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Balal,
Out of curiosity, I simulated data using the parameters reported and assuming a variance of 1 for the higher order factor.  I then fit the model shown in the diagram, assuming that the above variance was estimated, that the loading of Fluid Reasoning was fixed to 1, and that the unique variance was freely estimated and rounded to 0.  I obtained df = 92.

> Nc <- (16 * 17) / 2
+ ho_var <- 1
+ ho_load <- 4
+ ho_unique <- 5
+ load <- 16
+ cross_load <- 2
+ unique <- 16
+ Np <- ho_var + ho_load + ho_unique + load + cross_load + unique
+ df <- Nc - Np
+ Nc; Np; df
[1] 136
[1] 44
[1] 92
>

When I fit the model, the summary returned the above 92 df.  Lavaaan did not provide standard errors, which probably reflects the fact that the scales of the first-order factors have not been fixed.  However, the standardized estimates recovered the parameters within about .01 (with N = 5000) with the exception of the smallest cross-loading (within .04).

Is it possible that the authors reported parameter estimates from an analysis with no fixed scales and no standard errors?

My suggestion would be to follow these three steps:
1. Search the surrounding text for any further clues about how the models were fit.
2. Failing that, check the manual for references to other sources that might explain the analysis in more detail.
3. Failing that, write to the authors and ask for their script, output, or further explanation of the analysis.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.

  SAS 9.3 is the current version, which makes the hypothesis of reporting a model without fixed scales implausible.  That kind of thing was more common in the early days of SEM.  The improprieties in the path diagram made me wonder if it was a legacy analysis that had been copied over from edition to edition, but that is not the case if they used SAS 9.3.

  SAS has done a good job of making their docs available online.

https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/63962/HTML/default/viewer.htm#statug_calis_sect065.htm

messages.body_plain:
> I don't think they're fixed for identification because the variance estimates are different for each item and each factor.

They are neither estimated nor fixed when parameterization = "delta" (the default); they are not model parameters at all.  The residual variances are implied by the facts that (a) the total SD is fixed to 1 (visible under Scales y* in the summary() output) and (b) the common-factor variance and factor loading implies what proportion of the latent item-responses (unknown) variance is due to the common factor (visible via setting summary(..., rsquare = TRUE)).

> But what I don't understand is how come all the items and factors have the variances' estimates, but only the 8 factors have the values for std.err, z-value, and p value, whereas the 42 items have blanks for std.err, z-value, and p values?

Because the common-factor variances have been estimated, whereas the residual item variances are simply implied by other model parameters rather than estimated.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I am wondering how to fix thresholds (as constants) in lavaan.

See the ?model.syntax help page.

MODEL <- '
  f =~ 0.953*x1 + 1.676*x2   # fixed loadings
  f ~~ NA*f                  # free variances
  f ~  NA*1                  # free mean
  x1 | -4.606*t1 + -2.076*t2 # fixed thresholds
  x2 |     NA*t1 +     NA*t2 # free thresholds (intended?)
'

Hopefully you understand all the implications of your model, and how many statistically equivalent specifications there can be that represent different ideas about why your x1-by-x2 frequency tables follows its observed pattern.

messages.subject_clean: bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
> how to get the ECV in lavaan or is this the same as in the output under 'Latent Variances' ??

No, those would be variances of common factors.  Proportions of each observed-variable's variance explained by all predictors (i.e., all factors onto which it loads) can be found with summary(fit, rsquare = TRUE).  But the ancient idea of a single combined ECV per "factor" comes from a principal-components and later EFA history, where they are all orthogonal.  That is not a general condition for CFAs, so although you bifactor model might very well have orthogonal factors.  If your factors are orthogonal, you could manually calculate the proportion of each observed-variable's variance uniquely explained by one factor.  The variance due to a factor (call it X) is that factor's variance times that item's squared loading.  The proportion is then X divided by (X + the item's residual variance).

You could ask on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> or CrossValidated <https://stats.stackexchange.com/> whether anyone knows how to find those indices, or how to calculate them manually from a model's estimates.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Do i have to exclude a suppressor and confounding variable from my sem model?
messages.subject_clean: Do i have to exclude a suppressor and confounding variable from my sem model?
messages.body_plain:
Walkywalky,
  This strikes me as an odd question.  The way I think about it is this:  The concept of suppression reflects an earlier milieu in which bivariate correlations were taken as fundamental and this led researchers to view with suspicion either regression weights or causal effects at variance with the bivariate correlations.  Today, the tables have turned.  Now causal effects are seen as fundamental and when they do not align with bivariate correlations, it is the correlations that are considered as misleading.

  It seems to me that you can safely conceptualize both variables as confounders, it is just that one or more of the effects differ in sign.  If you omit the confounders from the equation for the DV of interest, then your estimates of causal effects are biased.  If you include them, then they might still be biased, but they are at least not biased by the two known sources of bias.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

I'm sure this is an extremely basic question - so I apologize. I'm new to SEM.  I've read and read about latent variables (=~) and covarying (~~), but I still don't understand the difference.  I thought latent variables measured the variance and covariance between and among items.  So, I thought that this:

KP =~ Q2 + Q5 + Q7 + Q9

would be the same thing as this:

Q2~~ Q5 + Q7 + Q9
Q5 ~~ Q7 + Q9
Q7 ~~ Q9

But when I ran a model using the second code, I got significantly higher fit indices than when I ran the model using the first code.

Why is that? Clearly I don't understand the difference between latent variables and covarying.  If someone can point me to some resources that can explain the difference in my example models above, I'd really appreciate it.

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: =~ versus ~~
messages.subject_clean: =~ versus ~~
messages.body_plain:
The second syntax imposes no constraints on the covariance matrix of the four observed variables. There are as many free parameters (6 covariances plus variances) as there are unique elements of the covariance matrix. the first syntax specifies that all covariances among the observed variables are accounted for by their joint dependence on a single common factor. This syntax specifies only 8 free parameters (4 loadings plus 4 residual variances). The nature of the constraints involves proportional ratios of covariances. For any two congeneric observed variables (loading on the same single common factor and without residual covariances), it must be true that:

covariance (1, 3) / covariance (2, 3) = constant across all other third variables.

messages.body_plain:
You didn't post your syntax, but the path diagram does show that you are not fitting a CFA model, which is all this function was designed to write syntax for (see the description at the top of the help page).  If you search for the word "regressions" in the Details part of the help page, you will see that this keyword is intended to indicate loadings of latent indicators of a higher-order factor.

Your model does not conform to what this function was designed for.  You can just omit the observed outcomes, and run CFA models to test invariance.  After you do that, you can print the syntax with as.character() to copy/paste and adapt to fit your structural model (including the extra variables that do not have a measurement model).  And if you stop setting return.fit=TRUE and use the function as a didactic tool (as I hoped people would use it) to see how to use lavaan syntax to fix/free/equate parameters, you can see how to label your parameters and test equivalence of regression slopes by writing that part of the syntax yourself.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> I'm able to extract the parameters from model 1 and save them as values, but then lavaan doesn't recognize those values in model 2.

messages.body_plain:
I highly recommend Keivit's article and scripts on OSF (https://osf.io/4bpmq/), Henk & Castro-Schilo 2016 along with McArdle's 2009 annual rev is good.

None of this is worth it, if you don't have multiple tasks probing the same construct at both timepoints (it's okay to have missing data). Mauricio's code is the equivalent of subtracting t2 from t1 and looking at the relationship of that to your groups (delta ~ group), there's no point to do that in lavaan unless you'll do more (be careful in your interpretation; i.e. reversion to the mean).

If you only have 1 task pre and post and your treatment was randomized consider just using residualized-change in a linear model (t2 ~ randomized_IV + t1).

I'm not an expert on causality, yet I remember reading issues when you only have 2 timepoints (e.g. pre, post). Another consideration is that you need to have at least strong longitudinal measurement invariance (see keivit's scripts for strict).

Best,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: Total percentage of explained variance in a CFA model?
messages.subject_clean: Total percentage of explained variance in a CFA model?
messages.body_plain:
Anouck,
  LISREL developers attempted something like this based on the determinants of the covariance matrix and the residual covariance matrix.  You can find criticism in Chapter 6 of Leslie Hayduk's book LISREL: Issues, debates and strategies (1996, JHU Press).  The basic problem is that it involves reducing a multivariate phenomenon, assuming you have more than one endogenous variable, to a single number.  Imagine accounting for X% of the variance in two orthogonal outcome variables.  Now imagine the same X% accounted for in two perfectly correlated variables.  How should the total variance explained score reflect such differences?

  As an alternative, consider reporting a summary of the individual R-square values.  At minimum, report their range.  Better yet, report a five number summary to describe their distribution.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)

fitRsquares <- lavInspect(fit, what='rsquare')
summary(fitRsquares)[-4]

Keith
------------------------

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.subject_clean: Multigroup CFA - problems with strong invariance estimation
messages.body_plain:
You have ordered indicators, so you need to start by constraining thresholds (at which point you need to freely estimate the intercepts and residual variances that are fixed in Group 2 for identification -- this necessitates using parameterization = "theta" in all models). If you have only 3 categories, this should be equivalent to your configural model (i.e., you just trade 2 thresholds for those 2 estimates).  If you have only 2 categories, you can't distinguish these levels of invariance, so you just simultaneously constrain thresholds, loadings, and intercepts to test strong variance (compared to the default configural model).

See examples in the ?semTools::measEq.syntax help page (after installing semTools), and read the Wu & Estabrook (2016) reference therein.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

You didn't post your syntax, but the path diagram does show that you are not fitting a CFA model, which is all this function was designed to write syntax for (see the description at the top of the help page).  If you search for the word "regressions" in the Details part of the help page, you will see that this keyword is intended to indicate loadings of latent indicators of a higher-order factor.

Your model does not conform to what this function was designed for.  You can just omit the observed outcomes, and run CFA models to test invariance.  After you do that, you can print the syntax with as.character() to copy/paste and adapt to fit your structural model (including the extra variables that do not have a measurement model).  And if you stop setting return.fit=TRUE and use the function as a didactic tool (as I hoped people would use it) to see how to use lavaan syntax to fix/free/equate parameters, you can see how to label your parameters and test equivalence of regression slopes by writing that part of the syntax yourself.

messages.subject: Re: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.subject_clean: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.body_plain:
This is an important issue.  Hox (2010, see chapter 14) advocates the use of level-specific fit estimates, and Ryu (2009, with West; 2014) provides steps for doing so.  It's nice that lavaan provides level-specific SRMR estimates (as does Mplus), as it seems a fairly simple thing to do because standardized residuals matrices are available at both levels.  Getting fit-specific versions of RMSEA and CFI, on the other hand, requires another set of models, one with the hypothesized model and another with the saturated model at the other level.  So if one were interested in the between level, the saturated model is at the within level and the between level is the hypothesized model.  The same is true for the independence model (variances on the diagonal, 0s otherwise).  I'd love to lavaan build in these level-specific fit statistics, as they are generally among the most frequently reported.

messages.subject: Re: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite
messages.subject_clean: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite
messages.body_plain:
> I had first warnings because of a high variance in my data. I performed a z-standardization

Bad idea, that biases your SEs and inflates Type I error rates.

https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3daa/5151f6a0931e9b6587cf06571486013f56ec.pdf

Divide or multiply by a constant (e.g., a factor of 10 or 100) instead of by a sample-based estimate.

> now I have the error
> Error in lav_samplestats_icov(COV = cov[[g]], ridge = ridge, x.idx = x.idx[[g]],  :
>   lavaan ERROR: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite

If your sample covariance matrix is NPD, there are either redundant variables or some variables with no variance.  This should have nothing whatsoever to do with standardizing/transforming your variables.   Does this occur when you use test = "standard"?  If not, then it probably happens when a bootstrap sample is drawn that coincidentally has all the same values for a particular variable, or in some way produces a NPD matrix.  If it does still occur without bootstrapping, the problem is in your original data, so I recommend investigating the correlation matrix among your modeled variables.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.subject_clean: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.body_plain:
> I'd love to lavaan build in these level-specific fit statistics, as they are generally among the most frequently reported.

The problem with providing chi-squared-based fit indices for each "model block" (e.g., for each level of analysis of a MLSEM or in each group of a multigroup model) is that such models typically involve placing equality constraints across blocks, to test hypotheses about process across blocks or to impose measurement invariance across blocks.  In such cases, the overall chi-squared is indeed a sum of chi-squared contributions from different model blocks, but the degrees of freedom can no longer be determined per block.  Because all chi-squared-based fit indices involve accounting for the df in some way, it would only be possible to provide them per block in unconstrained (e.g., configural-invariance) models.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: lavaan error: number of observations too small to compute Gamma in MGCFA using WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
> When it comes to my data, they are not normally distributed (Mardia coefficient: b2d= 519.104 / z=51.119 / p=0.00 ).

With N > 1400, you have a lot of power to detect minor deviations, so the test is not very informative on its own.

> Whenever I want to do a MGCFA on young adults and eldery patients, I get the lavaan error message:
> In lav_samplestats_from_data(lavdata = lavdata, missing = lavoptions$missing,  :
>
>   lavaan WARNING: number of observations (83) too small to compute Gamma
>
>
> Therefore, I have a few questions:
>
> 1) What is Gamma and do I need it to test the scale's invariance depending on the age of the participants?

As described on the ?lavInspect help page, Gamma is the asymptotic covariance matrix of the sample statistics.  A parameter's point estimate is accompanied by a SE, which is an estimate of its sampling variability across repeated samples from the same population.  Multiple parameters not only vary but covary (i.e., correlate across samples), leading to an estimated sampling-covariance matrix.  Gamma is needed for some calculations (I forget which), but Gamma can only be calculated if you have enough information from your data.  With 16 items on 5-point scales, you have 16*15/2 polychoric correlations + 16*4 thresholds = 184 sample statistics in each group, which is way larger than your 2 small Ns.

If you still get test statistics from your models and can use lavTestLRT() to compare models, then I'm guessing the Gamma is not needed for those calculations.

> 2) Can I use the MLR estimator instead (or any other estimator)?

A barplot() of each variable would show you how asymmetric the distributions are.  If each variable is approximately symmetric and each response category has a large enough N, then treating these as continuous with a robust ML estimator would give you approximately unbiased results about your factor loadings/correlations, as well as test statistics with approximately nominal Type I error rates.

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

Unfortunately, I don't know of any studies about treating ordinal data as continuous in the context of testing invariance, especially with a major imbalance in sample sizes.  ML might avoid the issue with Gamma, but you would still have smaller Ns in those 2 groups that the number of sample statistics: 16*19/2 = 152 sample stats.

>
> 3) I know that one of the solutions is to increase the number of participants, the problem is I can't do that since I'm analysing the data from a project that is over now. What are my other options instead?

I think you could try both estimators (robust ML and robust DWLS).   If they both lead to the same conclusions, that adds a little extra confidence.  And if invariance constraints hold (i.e., null hypotheses are not rejected), then that stabilizes the estimates because there are fewer of them and they are using information from all groups instead of one.  But the big problem is still the small Ns: with so little information about those populations, you have very little power to detect truly meaningful violations of invariance (unless the violations are huge).  So Type II error rates will probably be large.

If the models fit well in each sample and you have simple structure (no cross-loadings or correlated residuals across factors), you could test invariance for each factor separately to decrease the number of estimated parameters in your models (and the number of sample stats, which might resolve the Gamma issue).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrance,

You are right, of course.  But I wonder if you might take a look at something.  In the code below, I use the Peet family data from Hox (2002) and specify a path model of cards -> wordlist -> figures -> animals at both levels of analysis.  I used Ryu's (2009, 2014) partially saturated method to get level-specific RMSEA estimates. In the first case (Model 1), estimates are free to vary across levels.  Models 1a and 1b are the partially saturated between and within models, respectively.  In the second set of models (Model 2), I constrained the first path to be equal across levels.  I took that estimate from Model 2 (.435) and fixed the partially saturated models to that value, then computed RMSEA for each.  Judging by the full model fit stats, the model doesn't fit well but the level-specific indices show that the fit is acceptable at the within level but not the between.  I'm interested in your thoughts on this procedure.

Joe

peet.dat<-foreign::read.dta("https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/stat/stata/examples/mlm_ma_hox/peetcomp.dta")

# cards -> wordlist -> figures -> animals

#quick function to get rmsea by level
#bhws = between hypothesized/within saturated
#bhws = between saturated/within hypothesized
fit.stats.test <- function(bhws, bswh) {

  #between
  rmsea.b <- sqrt(
    max(
      (fitMeasures(bhws)["chisq"]-fitMeasures(bhws)["df"])/
        (fitMeasures(bhws)["df"]*lavInspect(bhws,"nclusters")-1),
      0))

  #within
  rmsea.w <- sqrt(
    max(
      (fitMeasures(bswh)["chisq"]-fitMeasures(bswh)["df"])/
        (fitMeasures(bswh)["df"]*lavInspect(bhws,"nobs")-lavInspect(bhws,"nclusters")),
      0))

  cbind(chisq.b=fitmeasures(bhws)["chisq"],df.b=fitmeasures(bhws)["df"], rmsea.b, srmr.b=fitmeasures(bhws)["srmr_between"],
        chisq.w=fitmeasures(bswh)["chisq"],df.w=fitmeasures(bswh)["df"], rmsea.w, srmr.w=fitmeasures(bswh)["srmr_within"])

}

#fit full model

model1 <- '

level: 1
cards ~ wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures

level: 2
cards ~ wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures
'

model1.out <- sem(model1, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model1.out)
fitmeasures(model1.out)[c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

#within saturated
model1a <- '

level: 1
cards ~~ cards + wordlist + figures + animals
wordlist ~~ wordlist + figures + animals
figures ~~ figures + animals
animals ~~ animals

level: 2
cards ~ wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures
'

model1a.out <- sem(model1a, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model1a.out)
fitmeasures(model1a.out)[c("chisq", "df", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

#between saturated
model1b <- '

level: 1
cards ~ wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures

level: 2
cards ~~ cards + wordlist + figures + animals
wordlist ~~ wordlist + figures + animals
figures ~~ figures + animals
animals ~~ animals
'

model1b.out <- sem(model1b, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model1b.out)
fitmeasures(model1b.out)[c("chisq", "df", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

#print fit stats
fit.stats.test(model1a.out, model1b.out)

#path a constrained across levels
model2 <- '

level: 1
cards ~ a*wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures

level: 2
cards ~ a*wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures
'

model2.out <- sem(model2, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model2.out)
fitmeasures(model2.out)[c("chisq", "df", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

model2a <- '

level: 1
cards ~~ cards + wordlist + figures + animals
wordlist ~~ wordlist + figures + animals
figures ~~ figures + animals
animals ~~ animals

level: 2
cards ~ .435*wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures
'

model2a.out <- sem(model2a, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model2a.out)
fitmeasures(model2a.out)[c("chisq", "df", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

model2b <- '
level: 1
cards ~ .435*wordlist
figures ~ wordlist
animals ~ figures

level: 2
cards ~~ cards + wordlist + figures + animals
wordlist ~~ wordlist + figures + animals
figures ~~ figures + animals
animals ~~ animals
'

model2b.out <- sem(model2b, data=peet.dat, cluster = "family")

summary(model2b.out)
fitmeasures(model2b.out)[c("chisq", "df", "fmin","rmsea","cfi","srmr_within","srmr_between")]

fit.stats.test(model2a.out, model2b.out)

I showed you the correct code in the previous email, except that I made a typo in the strict invariance model.  Strict invariance should additionally constrain residual variances, not intercepts (the latter are fixed to zero by default, so they are already equal).

group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings","residuals")

> Or should I use this code:

The only reason to use measEq.syntax() would be to learn about the model specification and lavaan syntax, so leave the default return.fit=FALSE so you can print the syntax and see what is happening.  This is a pedagogical tool.

> If the latter is correct, which ID.fac and ID.cat settings are best to use in my case

ID.cat should always be the default (following Wu & Estabrook, 2016), but with binary indicators the choice is arbitrary (the model specification would be statistically equivalent to lavaan's default specification).  ID.fac is arbitrary unless a level of invariance is rejected, in which case tests for partial invariance could be biased using the reference-indicator/marker-variable method if that indicator in fact has DIF; so either the default std.lv <http://std.lv> or effects.coding would be smarter if you need to test for partial invariance.

messages.subject: Re: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.subject_clean: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe,

Interesting approach, consistent with Ryu & West (2009), except that you have an estimated parameter that is shared across levels in Model 2 (which is then fixed in 2a and 2b).  That estimate is based on information at both levels, so it doesn't seem correct to attribute an entire degree of freedom to either level of analysis.  MLSEM is a bit outside my comfort zone, but here are some additional thoughts:
Fixing the parameter to its Model-2 estimate might seem like it will yield the same model-implied covariance matrix at that level, but it does not.  Compare the parameterEstimates() from each level's partially saturated model to the simultaneously estimated model, and you will notice that the within-level estimates remain quite similar, yet the between-level estimates change quite drastically (no doubt related to the dangerously small Level-2 N=37, although the Level-1 N=187 is also dangerously small for an MLSEM). Thus, the fit you derive from the partially saturated models does not actually reflect the (local?) fit of that level's model in the simultaneous estimation, especially in the between-level case.
PE2  <- parameterEstimates(model2.out , se=F)
PE2a <- parameterEstimates(model2a.out, se=F)
PE2b <- parameterEstimates(model2b.out, se=F)
## store partially-saturated model estimates next to originals
PE2$saturated[PE2$level == 1L] <- PE2b$est[PE2b$level == 1L]
PE2$saturated[PE2$level == 2L] <- PE2a$est[PE2a$level == 2L]
PE2
In normal-theory MLE, use N rather than N-1 in the RMSEA formula.  N-1 is based on old-school Wishart theory that is a leftover from the days of pure covariance-structure analysis (and that incomplete formula for F_ML still gets embarrassingly repeated in new SEM textbooks).
The N above has little affect on the estimated RMSEA value, even in small-N cases like this example.  But I think the more important issue is just whether the RMSEA formula applied at each level will yield a consistent, unbiased estimator of a population value (epsilon) at each level of analysis.  I haven't even seen epsilon defined at each level, and I'm not sure how it would be since the definitions are all the square-root of the discrepancy function over the df.  There is only one discrepancy function (and on df) for the whole model.
I don't think there is a level-specific discrepancy function, and unlike multigroup models, there is not a level-specific contribution to the model's chi-squared.  In single-level analyses, we can calculate the discrepancy between predictions and observations (i.e., model-implied and observed covariance matrices).  We haven't observed the covariance matrix at each level of analysis in multilevel data.  The model fit statistic is a likelihood ratio test calculated by comparing the log-likelihoods of the (whole simultaneously estimated) model and a completely saturated model.  The latter provides estimates of the level-specific covariance matrices, and each level's estimated matrix is sensitive to how the other level of the model is specified (just like the target-model estimates changed above).
I already found Ryu & West's use of the number of clusters in the Level-2 RMSEA formula to be suspect, but until this example I didn't have a clear idea why it made me uncomfortable.  The previous bullet point makes me doubt that it is as simple as saying "37 clusters contributed to the estimate of the between-cluster covariance matrix."  All data points are used to estimate matrices at both levels -- we choose estimates at both levels that maximize the likelihood of the observed data.  This is related to the larger point that observed cluster means (whose covariance matrix would be a more-biased estimate of the one obtained by fitting a 2-level saturated model) are merely estimates of true cluster means, which are latent variables (see Oliver Lüdtke and colleagues' 2008 and 2011 work on this, linked below).  I expect someone much smarter than I will eventually show that the level-specific chi-squared-based fit indices proposed by Ryu & West yield inconsistent, possibly consistently biased estimates of parameters that might not even have a formal definition outside of an ideal hypothetical scenario -- but I would be happier if someone shows the opposite :-)
My last observation is that even the SRMRs were not zero for the levels that were saturated.  Again, I suspect this is because one level's saturated-model estimates probably differ depending on how the other level's model is specified. messages.body_plain:
> when binary items are used, the best approach is to directly test for strict invariance by constraining thresholds, loadings and residuals?

You can still test strong invariance first (constrained thresholds and loadings; by virtue of fixing intercepts to 0 for identification, they are already equal).  But if strong invariance fits significantly worse than configural invariance, even if you narrow it down to a violation in one specific indicator, you have no way of knowing whether the violation of invariance is due to differences in that item's loading, intercept, or threshold.  I posted my slides, which explain why:

messages.body_plain:
> Given that the strict model fits nicely, can I just exclude the configural and strong tests and assume strict invariance?

This is a general question better suited for SEMNET.

All conclusions are tentative in science; the more evidence is gathered in support (or that does not refute) a conclusion, the more confidence we can have.  If your models don't converge, you don't have the opportunity to falsify your hypothesis of invariance.  You could argue the decent approximate fit is at least not evidence against the null hypothesis that strict invariance is a decent approximation to the truth.  Since misfit is statistically signifcant, you could still look for a partial invariance model by freeing the thresholds, loadings, and residuals for one item at a time using the group.partial= argument.

> What may cause the problems with the configural and strong models?

No idea.  My first guess would have been a small sample, but you have large N in both groups.  My only other guess would be such poor fit that a solution can't be found, but your fit is admittedly not that poor.  However, global fit indices can mask a lot of important local misfit.  Try looking at the lavResiduals() output from your strict model to see which parts of your model fail.  Even if SRMR is fairly low, that is just an average, which could be due to several near-zero residuals and one or two very large ones that could point to why a solution is hard to find (no guarantees).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.subject_clean: SRMR index in multilevel models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

Thanks for your thoughtful and helpful comments. To be fair to Ryu, she (and West) did not discuss cross-level constraints. The code I provided is my solution to that problem. As for the RMSEA formula, I sure did get it from a textbook, but I will not name the author! But yes, it seems a common and persistent mistake.

When I first started getting into level-specific fit statistics, I had only Mplus to work with – Yves had yet to drop the multilevel version of lavaan. It is been a while, but I did compare the estimates from the two programs and it seems the phenomena are not software specific. Of course that requires more testing.

In the end, I suspect we will have better level-specific fit statistics for multilevel structural equation modeling. It would be good to know the extent to which the model fits at each level of analysis. We do know that the within level contributes more information to the fitting function simply because of sample size and that the standard errors at the between level are necessarily smaller because means usually display less variability than do raw scores. Suzanne Jak has done interesting work in this area.

I am not a member of SEMNET but perhaps I should be. If some of these issues are above your pay grade then that is doubly true for me! Still, these developments are quite important to my work and will try to keep up on what is happening in the field.

Best,

Joe

> On Sep 18, 2019, at 1:07 PM, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi Joe,
>
> Interesting approach, consistent with Ryu & West (2009), except that you have an estimated parameter that is shared across levels in Model 2 (which is then fixed in 2a and 2b).  That estimate is based on information at both levels, so it doesn't seem correct to attribute an entire degree of freedom to either level of analysis.  MLSEM is a bit outside my comfort zone, but here are some additional thoughts:
> Fixing the parameter to its Model-2 estimate might seem like it will yield the same model-implied covariance matrix at that level, but it does not.  Compare the parameterEstimates() from each level's partially saturated model to the simultaneously estimated model, and you will notice that the within-level estimates remain quite similar, yet the between-level estimates change quite drastically (no doubt related to the dangerously small Level-2 N=37, although the Level-1 N=187 is also dangerously small for an MLSEM). Thus, the fit you derive from the partially saturated models does not actually reflect the (local?) fit of that level's model in the simultaneous estimation, especially in the between-level case.
> PE2  <- parameterEstimates(model2.out , se=F)
> PE2a <- parameterEstimates(model2a.out, se=F)
> PE2b <- parameterEstimates(model2b.out, se=F)
> ## store partially-saturated model estimates next to originals
> PE2$saturated[PE2$level == 1L] <- PE2b$est[PE2b$level == 1L]
> PE2$saturated[PE2$level == 2L] <- PE2a$est[PE2a$level == 2L]
> PE2
> In normal-theory MLE, use N rather than N-1 in the RMSEA formula.  N-1 is based on old-school Wishart theory that is a leftover from the days of pure covariance-structure analysis (and that incomplete formula for F_ML still gets embarrassingly repeated in new SEM textbooks).
> The N above has little affect on the estimated RMSEA value, even in small-N cases like this example.  But I think the more important issue is just whether the RMSEA formula applied at each level will yield a consistent, unbiased estimator of a population value (epsilon) at each level of analysis.  I haven't even seen epsilon defined at each level, and I'm not sure how it would be since the definitions are all the square-root of the discrepancy function over the df.  There is only one discrepancy function (and on df) for the whole model.
> I don't think there is a level-specific discrepancy function, and unlike multigroup models, there is not a level-specific contribution to the model's chi-squared.  In single-level analyses, we can calculate the discrepancy between predictions and observations (i.e., model-implied and observed covariance matrices).  We haven't observed the covariance matrix at each level of analysis in multilevel data.  The model fit statistic is a likelihood ratio test calculated by comparing the log-likelihoods of the (whole simultaneously estimated) model and a completely saturated model.  The latter provides estimates of the level-specific covariance matrices, and each level's estimated matrix is sensitive to how the other level of the model is specified (just like the target-model estimates changed above).
> I already found Ryu & West's use of the number of clusters in the Level-2 RMSEA formula to be suspect, but until this example I didn't have a clear idea why it made me uncomfortable.  The previous bullet point makes me doubt that it is as simple as saying "37 clusters contributed to the estimate of the between-cluster covariance matrix."  All data points are used to estimate matrices at both levels -- we choose estimates at both levels that maximize the likelihood of the observed data.  This is related to the larger point that observed cluster means (whose covariance matrix would be a more-biased estimate of the one obtained by fitting a 2-level saturated model) are merely estimates of true cluster means, which are latent variables (see Oliver Lüdtke and colleagues' 2008 and 2011 work on this, linked below).  I expect someone much smarter than I will eventually show that the level-specific chi-squared-based fit indices proposed by Ryu & West yield inconsistent, possibly consistently biased estimates of parameters that might not even have a formal definition outside of an ideal hypothetical scenario -- but I would be happier if someone shows the opposite :-)
> My last observation is that even the SRMRs were not zero for the levels that were saturated.  Again, I suspect this is because one level's saturated-model estimates probably differ depending on how the other level's model is specified.  But I'll leave it to you to fit a fully saturated model and compare those estimates to the saturated components of your models 2a and 2b.  Why they would differ ... that's above my pay grade :-)  But I'd love if anyone could explain it to me/us by replying here!  Alternatively, you could post a question on SEMNET, which has a much broader audience; hopefully someone could shed more light on it.  Might also help to run the same examples in Mplus to verify that these phenomena are not software-specific.
> fitMeasures(model2a.out, c("srmr_within","srmr_between")) # saturated within
>  srmr_within srmr_between
>        0.029        0.328
> fitMeasures(model2b.out, c("srmr_within","srmr_between")) # saturated between
>  srmr_within srmr_between
>        0.036        0.026

messages.body_plain:
> To be fair to Ryu, she (and West) did not discuss cross-level constraints.

Right, that's all I meant by "consistent with ... except for ...".  Sorry, didn't mean to imply they had provided different (or any) advice about equality constraints across levels.

> As for the RMSEA formula, I sure did get it from a textbook, but I will not name the author! But yes, it seems a common and persistent mistake.

Oh, perhaps I was being too snarky.  I just get frustrated that textbooks only present SEM as it was conceived a generation ago, instead of in its current state.  For the same reason I get frustrated seeing 100-year-old ANOVA and t test formulas in stats textbooks that make those procedures seem different from regression, instead of teaching from a unifying model-comparison perspective like Maxwell & Delaney's or Judd et al.'s books do.

But the textbooks are not mistaken, just old fashioned.  LISREL and EQS (perhaps also SPSS Amos and SAS PROC CALIS? I don't use them) correctly use N-1 to calculate RMSEA because that is the multiplier they use to derive the chi-squared they report.  (Actually, I recall LISREL 8.4 provided 2 chi-squareds, one labeled "normal theory", so perhaps they do both now?  I only used it cursorily in grad school.)  Mplus uses N as the multiplier and in RSMEA because it includes mean structure by default, in which case Wishart theory isn't really appropriate because it is not longer purely covariance-structure analysis (Wishart describes sampling variability of covariance matrices).  lavaan() uses N by default (consistent with the default likelihood = "normal"), but you can request likelihood = "wishart" (or mimic = "eqs") to tell lavaan to use N-1 consistently in all calculations.

> I did compare the estimates from the two programs and it seems the phenomena are not software specific.

Good to know.

> It would be good to know the extent to which the model fits at each level of analysis.

Indeed, and the SRMRs at each level are for that purpose.  It is only the chi-squared-based indices that have some trouble here, even when there are no equality constraints across levels.

Something I didn't think to point out in the last message about your partially-saturated models:  I pointed out that the SRMRs for saturated portions are not zero, but also notice the SRMRs for the hypothesized-structure portions of Models 2a and 2b do not match the level-specific SRMRs that are already provided in the simultaneous Model 2.  Again, I think the simultaneous Model-2 SRMRs are the ones that provide what you are looking for, because those are calculated using level-specific covariance matrices from a fully saturated model that lavaan() internally fits (and are provided via the fitted() method).

This is not a unique situation to multilevel data. When FIML is used to fit a single-level model to data, the saturated model is also fit to provide the fitted() output and the basis for the chi-squared/LR test, as well as the SRMR.

> Suzanne Jak has done interesting work in this area.

We teach SEM together. I should ask her about writing a Teacher Corner article on these issues, hopefully to stimulate further development.

For now, I would offer that any overall fit index (even level-specific) is not going to be fully informative about the ways your model does/not fail to reproduce the data.  Individual standardized/correlation residuals are more informative, and can point to substantial problems that might be hidden by averaging across the whole model.

resid(model2.out, type = "cor.bentler")

Unfortunately, lavResiduals() does not yet work for multilevel data (but I think it is a fairly high priority to get it working), so you can't get the z tests for individual standardized residuals or the SRMR, but the descriptive information from the resid() method still provides very useful guidance.  The output from the example above indicates the within-level model only seems to substantially fail to reproduce the within-level variance of figures, but there are several even more substantial failures of the between-level model to reproduce figures and cards between-level variances, as well as their between-level covariances with each other and with other variables.  This is consistent with the overall level-specific fit you calculated, but I think there are fewer theoretical problems, and it is more informative about why the between model is inadequate.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence and members of the lavaan group.

So, following Torrence's suggestion, we went a litle bit further and Hugo actually put together a function to use your measEq.syntax and test also the structural invariance of the model. Will you please be kind to test it and see if there's some concept error that we may be missing?
This is function:

#Nested Models Invariance Across Groups. Fixing measEq.syntax for structural models.
ModelInvariance <- function(data, model, group, estimator, restrictions, meanstructure, std.lv <http://std.lv>, show.syntax){

  #Show which group is being tested
  if (show.syntax){
    cat("Displaying model invariance syntax:")} else {
    cat(paste("Testing model invariance for:",group,'\n'))}

  #Clean group cases in database
  data_subset <- data[ , group]
  data <- data[complete.cases(data_subset), ]

  #Splits model between structural and measurement
  splitmodel <- strsplit(model,'\n')[[1]] #Splits all lines
  splitmodel <- splitmodel[-grep("#", splitmodel)] #Removes lines with comments

  #Structural model in lines
  structural_model <- splitmodel[grepl('~', splitmodel)&!grepl('~~', splitmodel)&!grepl('=~', splitmodel)]

  #Measurement model as a single string
  measurement_model <- paste(splitmodel[!(grepl('~', splitmodel)&!grepl('~~', splitmodel)&!grepl('=~', splitmodel))], collapse='\n')

  #Prepares structural model syntax
  nsml <- length(structural_model) #Number of Structural Model Lines
  if (nsml>0){ #skips processing the structural model if there is none
    nsmlarray <- (1:nsml) #Array of the Number of Structural Model Lines
    groupnum <- length(unique(data[[group]])) #Number of groups
    grouparray <- (1:groupnum) #Array of the number of groups
    g <- paste('.g', grouparray,sep='') #Group list: '.g1' '.g2' '.gn'
    lhs <- sub('~.*', '', structural_model) #Left hand side list
    rhs <- sub('.*~', '', structural_model) #Right hand side list
    #Creates all combinations of lhs and rhs with the "+" operator
    nlhs=c()
    nrhs=c()
    plusmask <- grepl('\\+', lhs)|grepl('\\+', rhs) #Logical vector of lines that have a "+"
    for (line in nsmlarray){
      if (plusmask[line]){
        splitlhs <- unlist(strsplit(lhs[line],"\\+"))
        splitrhs <- unlist(strsplit(rhs[line],"\\+"))
        for (part in splitlhs){
          nlhs <- c(nlhs, rep(part, length(splitrhs))) #stores combinations of lhs
          nrhs <- c(nrhs, splitrhs) #stores combinations of rhs
        }
      }
    }
    lhs <- c(lhs[!plusmask], nlhs) #Replaces old lhs with new lhs
    rhs <- c(rhs[!plusmask], nrhs) #Replaces old rhs with new rhs

    nsml <- length(lhs) #New Number of structural model lines
    nsmlarray <- (1:nsml) #Array of the number of structural model lines

    #Creates the variant structural model syntax:ex. 'DI ~ c(gama.1.g1, gama.1.g2)*MBI' 'AP ~ c(gama.2.g1,   gama.2.g2)*MBI'
    gama <- c()
    space <- c(rep(', ',groupnum-1), '')
    for (line in nsmlarray){
      gama <- c(gama, paste('gama.',line, g, space, sep='', collapse=''))}
      gama <- paste(lhs, ' ~ c(', gama , ')*', rhs, sep='') #gama = Lines of the variant structural model
      var.structural.model <- paste(gama, collapse='\n')#Model sintax as a single string

    #Creates the invariant structural model syntax:ex. 'DI ~ c(gama.1, gama.1)*MBI' 'AP ~ c(gama.2, gama.2)*MBI'
    invargama <- c()
    for (line in nsmlarray){
      invargama <- c(invargama, paste('gama.',line, space, sep='', collapse=''))}
    invargama <- paste(lhs, ' ~ c(', invargama , ')*', rhs, sep='')#invargama = Lines of the invariant structural model
    invar.structural.model <- paste(invargama, collapse='\n')#Model sintax as a single string
    } else {
    var.structural.model=c()
    invar.structural.model=c()} #end of structural model syntax

  #Creates a list of fitted nested models
  nested.models <- list()
  if (!show.syntax){cat("Fitted models:")}
  for (i in 1L:length(restrictions)) { #Creates model syntax for all restrictions imposed on the model
    #Latest restriction
    model.label <- restrictions[i]
    #Array of restrictions
    group.equal <- restrictions[0:i]
    #Creates the measurement model syntax
    measurement.model.syntax <- measEq.syntax(
      configural.model=measurement_model,
      data = data,
      estimator = estimator,
      parameterization = "theta",
      #ID.cat = "Wu",
      ID.fac = "ul",
      group = group,
      group.equal = group.equal,
      return.fit = F)
    if ("structural" %in% group.equal){
      #Adds invar.structural.model for structural invariant models
      model.syntax <- paste(measurement.model.syntax, '\n##STRUCTURAL:\n\n', invar.structural.model, sep='', collapse='\n')} else {
      #Adds var.structural.model for structural variant models
      model.syntax <- paste(measurement.model.syntax, '\n##STRUCTURAL:\n\n', var.structural.model, sep='', collapse='\n')}

    #Displays current model syntax if show.syntax == TRUE
    if (show.syntax){cat(paste("\n\n##### MODEL: ",model.label, ' #####\n', model.syntax))}

    #Fits current model
    else {current.model <- suppressWarnings(sem(model.syntax, data=data, meanstructure = meanstructure, std.lv <http://std.lv> = std.lv <http://std.lv>, estimator= estimator, group=group))
    #Displays latest fitted model
    cat(paste(' ', model.label, sep=''))
    #Compiles List of Fitted Models
    nested.models[[model.label]] <- current.model
  }}

    #Compares fitted nested models
  if (!show.syntax){
    cat("\nComparing fitted models, please wait...\n\n")
    suppressWarnings(compareFit(nested.models, nested = T, indices = T, argsLRT = list(fit.measures = "all")))}
}

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a data set with multiple dependent variables and multiple independent variables. In addition, the data is nested: there are multiple patches, and within each patch several individuals. The dependent variables were measured at the individual level, but independent variables were measured both at the individual and at the patch level. Those independent variables that were measured at the individual level may also be dependent on the independent variables that were measured at the patch level.
All my variables are continuous. The dependent variables are all supposed to represent the same phenomena, but when I tried creating a latent variables out of them it gave a poor fit (maybe because some of the measured variables are inverse to one another).
Though I don't have any latent variables, I thought that due to the complex structure of the data lavaan would be appropriate to use. I'd be happy to hear if this is not accurate and there are other packages that are more recommended for such a design.
My questions are:
1. Would it be more appropriate to account for the nestedness of the data by using a multilevel model in lavaan and using the patches as clusters, or to use lavaan.survey?
2. What are the appropriate fit indices to look at for multilevel models?
3. Are there any recommended packages for plotting lavaan models? Semplot works poorly when there are many variables and connections.
4. Is there an efficient way to estimate direct, indirect and total effects in lavaan? I know one can add equations in the syntax to do that, but for complex models this can be quite tedious.

Thanks for your help and attention,
Efrat

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model as follow:

riclpm<-'

#Latent mean structure with intercepts

#Random intercepts

RIL =~ 1*L3 + 1*L5 + 1*L11

RIB =~ 1*B3 + 1*B5 + 1*B11

#Intercepts

L3 ~ l3*1

L5 ~ l5*1

L11 ~ l11*1

B3 ~ b3*1

B5 ~ b5*1

B11 ~ b11*1

#Variances and covariance

RIL ~~ RIL

RIB ~~ RIB

RIL ~~ RIB

#Latent variables for AR and cross-lagged effects

FL3 =~ 1*L3

FL5 =~ 1*L5

FL11 =~ 1*L11

FB3 =~ 1*B3

FB5 =~ 1*B5

FB11 =~ 1*B11

# AR and cross-lagged effects

FL11 ~ FL5 + FB5

FL5 ~ FL3 + FB3

FB11 ~ FL5 + FB5

FB5 ~ FL3 + FB3

#Variances and covariances

FL3 ~~ FL3

FL5 ~~ FL5

FL11 ~~ FL11

FB3 ~~ FB3

FB5 ~~ FB5

FB11 ~~ FB11

FL3 ~~ FB3

FL5 ~~ FB5

FL11 ~~ FB11

'

riclpm.fit <- lavaan(riclpm, data = bidat,

              missing = 'ML',

              int.ov.free = F,

              int.lv.free = F,

              auto.fix.first = F,

              auto.fix.single = F,

              auto.cov.lv.x = F,

              auto.cov.y = F,

              auto.var = F)

I am very surprised with the very high covariance that I obtained between my two random intercepts: I get a RIL~~RIB estimate equal to -1.015 (Std.lv = -0.798, Std.all = -0.798). I do not understand how the covariance can be so high when the correlation between my measured variables L and B at each time are quite low: r(L3,B3)=-0.15; r(L5,B5)=-0.12; r(L11,B11)=-0.11. I am not sure how this is possible?

I tried to extract the RIL and RIB with lavPredict in order to try and understand better what is happening. I used the following code:

priclpm<-lavPredict(riclpm.fit, type="lv", method="regression", append.data=TRUE)

dpriclpm<-as.data.frame(priclpm)

cor(dpriclpm$RIL,dpriclpm$RIB)

cov(dpriclpm$RIL,dpriclpm$RIB)

plot(x=dpriclpm$RIL, y=dpriclpm$RIB)

The covariance between the RIL and RIB predicted by lavPredict is equal to -0.76, and the correlation is equal to -0.96. These results brought an additional question: I thought that the covariance between latent variables in std.lv <http://std.lv> and std.all could be understood as a correlation, since the variables are standardized. But then why don’t we observe the same value between the correlation computed by lavPredict and the std. covariance from the model?

Thank you in advance for your insights!

Ava

messages.subject: Re: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions
messages.subject_clean: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions
messages.body_plain:
> 1. Would it be more appropriate to account for the nestedness of the data by using a multilevel model in lavaan and using the patches as clusters, or to use lavaan.survey?

lavaan.survey() only corrects SEs and tests for clustering in a level-1 model (also available in lavaan() now, if you specify a cluster= variable for a single-level model).  You have Level-2 hypotheses (a patch-level IV predicts the patch-level component of an individual-level IV), so MLSEM seems more appropriate.

> 2. What are the appropriate fit indices to look at for multilevel models?

All the same fit indices are available, but it is recommended to evaluate fit at each level separately.  SRMRs are available at each level of analysis.

> 3. Are there any recommended packages for plotting lavaan models? Semplot works poorly when there are many variables and connections.

And I think it only plots MLSEMs from Mplus output; not sure about OpenMx or lavaan yet.

> 4. Is there an efficient way to estimate direct, indirect and total effects in lavaan? I know one can add equations in the syntax to do that, but for complex models this can be quite tedious.

No, but you can check to see if you missed any by multiplying the beta matrix (at either level) against itself 2, then 3, then ... p-1 times (the maximum number of sequential causal links).

B <- lavInspect(fit, "est")[[1]]$beta # level-1 beta
B %*% B        # 2-path indirect effects
B %*% B %*% B  # 3-path indirect effects

By the time you get a product full of zeros, you won't have any more indirect effects of higher order.  Each nonzero cell is the point estimate for an indirect effect whose path you can trace from the predictor (column variable) to the outcome (row variable).  To obtain the delta-method SEs, you can check that each nonzero cell in each product is represented in your model syntax.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Unified SEM with categorical data – Is this a correct approach?
messages.body_plain:
> I am considering all variables as exogenous categorical here. The model works in this case. Is this correct?

No, they are all endogenous.  You are specifying them all as single-indicators of corresponding latent factors.  Not sure why that is necessary.  You also don't need to fix all those regressions to zero; they are zero by default, unless you explicitly free them.  Your syntax could be a lot simpler:

##### Auto-regressive part – predict (t) with (t-1)

y5 ~ y1
y6 ~ y2
y7 ~ y3
y8 ~ y4

> 2. I know that some of the variables are binary and/or ordinal

According to your description, all of them.  But no distributional assumptions are required of exogenous predictors, so you could avoid defining the unnecessary "eta"s.

> so I did try declaring all variables as “ordered” and using the same model with the WLSMV estimator. The model does not converge in that case. If this is the right way to do it, how should I get it to work?

Use the sem() function to enable reasonable defaults.  Since you don't want to automatically estimate the residual covariances, you fix those to zero.

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I am testing for measurement invariance across two gender groups using permuteMeasEq. My dataset is composed of 800 responses to a 16-item instrument, with each item scored on a five-point Likert scale. On the basis of prior exploratory analyses, I am fitting a bifactor model with three factors plus a general factor. I am aware that measEq.syntax only has limited support for bifactor models, so have tried to follow all the recommendations from help files and examples. Based on my understanding of this <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/issues/60> exchange, I used ID.fac = "UV" and manually freed latent variable means when generating syntax (by replacing zeroes with NAs in the "## LATENT MEANS/INTERCEPTS:" portion of the syntax).

I am able to run permuteMeasEq analyses that compare the configural model to a null model, and also test for metric and scalar invariance. I have additionally run models that are partially invariant at the scalar level. There are apparently no issues with model convergence (and AFIs, incidentally, are very good).

However, when I attempt to test for threshold invariance - second in the sequence, after testing the configural model - I receive the following error: "Error in A %*% P.inv : requires numeric/complex matrix/vector arguments". I am unsure of what is causing this error.

I have attached the relevant syntax for reference, and am more than happy to provide any other useful information/files. I am running R version 3.5.0 on a Windows device, with semTools 0.5-2 and lavaan 0.6-5

Many thanks in advance,

Ryan

messages.body_plain:
Teresa,
  That was a nice feature of the original Mx program.  Here is how I would proceed for random start values.  You can then place the analysis in a loop and add a data frame to collect the information that you want from each iteration.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example (modified)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 '

# Create parameter table
HSParameterTable <- lavaanify(HS.model,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
HSParameterTable

# Create a functiont to generate start values
makeRandomStartValues <- function(...){
  sv1 <- 1
  sv2to3 <- runif(n=2, min=-1, max=1)
  sv4to7 <- runif(n=4, min=.1, max=2.1)
  return(c(sv1, sv2to3, sv4to7))
} # end makeRandomStartValues

# Insert the start values in a new parameter table
HSNewParameterTable <- HSParameterTable
HSNewParameterTable$ustart <- makeRandomStartValues()
HSNewParameterTable

# Fit model using new paramter table
fit <- lavaan(HSNewParameterTable, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit)
lavInspect(fit, what='start')

Keith

Keith A. Markus

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

 set.seed(0)
  D <- mapply(sample, 6, rep(18, 6), T) # DATA

 library(lavaan)                     # MODEL
 m1 <- " f1 = ~v1+v2+v3
         f2 = ~v4+v5+v6 "

fit1 <- cfa(m1, data = D)            # RUN lavaan

Hi Aiden,

For the latent interactions the moderator is the latent variable, not the indicators of the latent variable. So, for the purposes of probing the interaction you could look for values of the latent variable (hence -1, 0, and 1) not value of the original variable. This applies when latent variances are fixed to 1 to set the scale of the latent variables (and when latent means are set to 0), if you use another method to set the scale, you would use different values for the simple slopes.

Alex

Hi
I am not sure what is your mean by 'to put the highest estimate=1,000 and not the firs'. but i assume your mean is setting latent variable variance and mean to 1 and 0 prospectively for identification, instead of fixing the first indicator loading and intercept to 1 and 0. if so, for doing it simply use std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE in your cfa or sem function. for example:
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

if you want to put the loading of other indicator to 1 instead of the first one simply insert 1 before it in your model and insert NA* before the first one. for example:
model <- ’ ind60 =~ NA*x1 + x2 + 1*x3
                dem60 =~ NA*y1 + y2 + y3 + 1*y4
'
HTH

messages.subject_clean: Comparing factor scores
messages.body_plain:
The means of factor scores correspond to the (estimated) means of the
latent variables in the model.

In a single group analysis (which is what you seem to be doing), the
means for all latent variables are (by default) fixed to zero. As a
result, the factor scores also have zero means.

There are two things that puzzle me in your question:

1) if your goal is to compare latent means, you don't need factor scores
at all; you can estimate the latent means in your model directly

2) in a single-group, single-timepoint setting, the means of latent
variables are arbitrary, so there seems no point trying to compare them.

But perhaps we misunderstood your goal. Can you give us more background
on what you wish to accomplish?

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: The default option conditional.x = TRUE when using WLSMV for categorial endogenous variables.
messages.subject_clean: The default option conditional.x = TRUE when using WLSMV for categorial endogenous variables.
messages.body_plain:
On 9/27/19 3:59 AM, tran viet Yen wrote:
> Hello everyone in this group.
>
> Just a small question, could anyone let me know why the option

> ‘conditional.x = TRUE’ *is the default* when there are some categorical

> endogenous variables in the data

The reason is the following: suppose you have p=10 binary endogenous
variables (y), and q=10 continuous exogenous covariates (x). If
conditional.x = FALSE, we would need to compute 20*19//2 tetrachoric and
biserial correlations, in addition to 10 thresholds (for y), 10 means
for (x), and 10 variances (also for x). This gives 220 sample
statistics, leading to a weight matrix (W) of dimension 220 x 220.

If, on the other hand, we use conditional.x = TRUE, we 'regress out' the
x variables first, and we are left with 10*9/2 = 45 (residual)
tetrachoric correlations, and 10 (residual) thresholds. The dimension of
W is now only 55 x 55.

Therefore, when WLS(MV) is used with categorical endogenous variables,
we prefer conditional.x = TRUE because estimating a large W is
expensive, and requires a (much) larger sample size.

See also

Muthén, B. (1984). A general structural equation model with dichotomous,
ordered categorical, and continuous latent variable indicators.
Psychometrika, 49(1), 115-132.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Variance-covariance or correlation matrix?; Starting values?
messages.subject_clean: Variance-covariance or correlation matrix?; Starting values?
messages.body_plain:
On 9/25/19 9:27 PM, Teresa O. wrote:
> 1) Are (unstandardized) estimates in the lavaan output calculated using
> the variance-covariance matrix or the correlation matrix?

The covariance matrix. You could use 'std.ov = TRUE' to force lavaan to
use a correlation matrix instead (but currently, this correlations
matrix is still treated as if it were a covariance matrix).

> 2) How are the starting values selected by default within lavaan?

- for factor loadings, lavaan uses the FABIN3 estimator (from Hagglund,
1982) (this is an instrumental variables approach)

- residual variances (eg for indicators) are set to 0.5 times the
observed variance of indicator

- factor variances are set to 0.05

- regressions and covariances are set to 0.0

You can of course override this by specifying start()* modifiers for
individual parameters.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Modification indices inconsistency
messages.subject_clean: Modification indices inconsistency
messages.body_plain:
On 9/26/19 12:16 PM, Maksim Rudnev wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I ran a simple path analysis and got Chi-square of 5.5, then I requested
> modification indices and got one of the size 17.1. How's that possible?

The modification indices are based on the score test. The model
Chi-Square test is a likelihood ratio test (LRT). Only when the sample
size becomes very large, they will converge to the same value. In
particular in small samples, they may diverge.

Modification indices only give you roughly some information about the
impact of relaxing a single parameter (one at a time).

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear prof. Yves,

Thank you very much for the explanation with an example and the suggested reference. These strengthen my understanding on this issue.

If the variances/covariances of covariates do not contribute to the fitting function, then the model's estimates are more stable due to the reduced size of weight matrix. So basically the stability of estimates is improved at the cost of excluding out the contribution of covariates in the fitting function.

This trade-off is reasonable as the sample sizes generally are not enough for the estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix W of large size.

Best regards,

Yen.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Terrence,

Thank you for your quick response.

I have changed my null model now to the following with your suggestions. As all the variables are endogenous, should I be declaring (y1-y8) as "ordered" or just the ones which are being predicted (y5-y8)? I tried both combinations and the model is still not converging:

##### Regression model

y5 ~ y1
y6 ~ y2
y7 ~ y3
y8 ~ y4

# Variance
y1~~y1\n   y1~~y2\n   y1~~y3\n   y1~~y4\n
y2~~y2\n   y2~~y3\n   y2~~y4\n
y3~~y3\n   y3~~y4\n
y4~~y4\n
y5~~y5\n
y6~~y6\n
y7~~y7\n
y8~~y8

Is this correct? As its a unified SEM model, I care about the autoregressive as well as the contemporaneous relations.

Could you please explain more about what you mean by this? - "Use the sem() function to enable reasonable defaults."

Thanks,
Priyanka

On Mon, Sep 23, 2019 at 4:07 PM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I am considering all variables as exogenous categorical here. The model works in this case. Is this correct?
> No, they are all endogenous.  You are specifying them all as single-indicators of corresponding latent factors.  Not sure why that is necessary.  You also don't need to fix all those regressions to zero; they are zero by default, unless you explicitly free them.  Your syntax could be a lot simpler:
>
> ##### Auto-regressive part – predict (t) with (t-1)
> y5 ~ y1
> y6 ~ y2
> y7 ~ y3
> y8 ~ y4
>
>
> > 2. I know that some of the variables are binary and/or ordinal
> According to your description, all of them.  But no distributional assumptions are required of exogenous predictors, so you could avoid defining the unnecessary "eta"s.
>
> > so I did try declaring all variables as “ordered” and using the same model with the WLSMV estimator. The model does not converge in that case. If this is the right way to do it, how should I get it to work?
> Use the sem() function to enable reasonable defaults.  Since you don't want to automatically estimate the residual covariances, you fix those to zero.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: different results in Mplus and R?
messages.subject_clean: different results in Mplus and R?
messages.body_plain:
The two programs are estimating different numbers of parameters (34 in Mplus and 23 in lavaan). There are a number of reasons why this might occur (e.g. indicators are treated as categorical in Mplus but continuous in lavaan, exogenous predictors are treated as random in Mplus but fixed in lavaan). Working out this discrepancy will likely provide insight.

Alex

messages.subject: percentile bootstrap for sem()
messages.subject_clean: percentile bootstrap for sem()
messages.body_plain:
I am using lavvan to run a structural equation model. I would like to calculate standard errors for standardized indirect effects using the percentile boot strap method. Is it possible to specify this within the sem() function? I have specified that se="bootstrap" and missing="FIML" in my original sem() call. Based on the documentation for the package, I believe that the default for lavaan is to use the naive method for calculating boot straps. I understand that I can specify the type of boostrap using the boot.ci.type="perc" function within the parameterEstimates() function, however this gives a CI that corresponds to the unstandardized estimate as opposed to the standardized estimate (which is what I want) despite specifying standardized=T (this just additionally provides the standardized estimate as an additional column). Additionally, I tried to use the standardizedSolutions() function to obtain bootstrapped SEs and CIs, however I am unable to specify that I would like to use the percentile bootstrap.

Thank you!
